D1.1.1.q: A hospital's files are suddenly locked and a message demands payment in Bitcoin to unlock them. What kind of threat is this?
D1.1.1.why: Ransomware is malware that encrypts data and demands payment to release it.

D1.1.1.q: A program hidden inside a free game download secretly records everything the user types and sends it to a criminal. What threat is this?
D1.1.1.why: Spyware is malware that secretly records activity such as keystrokes, so passwords can be stolen.

D1.1.1.q: Which protection is aimed MOST directly at viruses and other malware?
options: Off-site backups in case of floods
Training staff to spot fake phone calls
Fire suppression in the server room
D1.1.1.why: Antivirus detects and removes malware; the others mainly protect against natural disasters, social engineering and fire.

D1.1.2.q: An attacker exploits an unpatched web server to get into a shop's network and download customer records. Which threat is this?
D1.1.2.why: Hacking is gaining access to a system without permission, often through unpatched weaknesses.

D1.1.2.q: Someone outside a company guesses an administrator's weak password and logs in to change prices on the website. Which threat is this?
D1.1.2.why: Getting into a system without permission, e.g. by guessing a password, is unauthorised access.

D1.1.2.q: Which is the best defence against hackers exploiting known flaws in a web server?
D1.1.2.why: Attackers target unpatched software, so applying updates closes the known flaws.

D1.1.3.q: A technician spills coffee over a server, which stops working and loses a day's orders. Which threat is this?
D1.1.3.why: Accidental damage is unintentional harm from human error or physical accidents.

D1.1.3.q: A cleaner unplugs a server to use the socket, and the database on it is corrupted. Which threat is this?
D1.1.3.why: Unintentional harm caused by human error is accidental damage.

D1.1.3.q: Which of these is accidental damage rather than a deliberate attack?
options: A laptop dropped down the stairs
D1.1.3.why: Accidental damage is unintentional; the others are deliberate attacks.

D1.1.4.q: Staff get an email that looks like it's from the IT department asking them to click a link and 'confirm' their password. What attack is this?
D1.1.4.why: Social engineering tricks people, not systems, into giving away information or access.

D1.1.4.q: Someone phones reception pretending to be from the IT supplier and asks for the admin password 'to fix a fault'. What is this?
D1.1.4.why: A phone call with a made-up story to get information is vishing and pretexting: social engineering.

D1.1.4.q: Why are social engineering attacks hard to stop with firewalls and antivirus alone?
options: They trick people rather than technology
They only happen during floods and fires
They always arrive on infected USB sticks
They only damage hardware, not data
D1.1.4.why: Social engineering attacks the human, so training (plus filtering and MFA) is the main defence.

D1.1.5.q: Lightning causes a power surge that destroys a company's server and the data on it. Which type of external threat is this?
D1.1.5.why: Floods, fires, earthquakes and lightning are natural disasters: they cannot be prevented, only prepared for.

D1.1.5.q: Which of these is a natural disaster threat to data?
options: An earthquake damaging a data centre
A virus spreading through email attachments
A member of staff emailing data to the wrong person
A hacker logging in with a stolen password
D1.1.5.why: An earthquake is a natural disaster. The others are malware, accidental disclosure and unauthorised access.

D1.2.1.q: An employee visits a film piracy site on a work PC, and malware is silently installed. Which internal threat is this?
D1.2.1.why: Visiting malicious or banned sites on work systems can bring malware in.

D1.2.2.q: A receptionist emails a spreadsheet of patient details to the wrong person by mistake. What is this?
D1.2.2.why: Sharing data by mistake still counts as a data breach.

D1.2.3.q: On his last day, a salesperson copies the whole customer database onto a USB stick to take to a rival. Which threat is this?
D1.2.3.why: It is a deliberate insider act of copying confidential data to share or sell.

D1.2.4.q: A nurse leaves an unencrypted USB stick of patient records on a train. Which internal threat does this show?
D1.2.4.why: USB sticks, laptops and phones can be lost or bring in malware.

D1.3.1.q: Ransomware encrypts a small firm's only copy of its accounts, and there is no backup. What is the most direct impact?
options: Loss of customers due to public image
D1.3.1.why: With no backup, the data is permanently lost or inaccessible.

D1.3.2.q: After failing to secure customer data, a company is fined by the ICO and sued by affected customers. What impact is this?
options: Financial loss due to legal action
Loss of customers due to public image
D1.3.2.why: ICO fines and lawsuits are financial losses caused by legal action.

D1.3.3.q: After a card data breach makes the news, shoppers stop trusting a retailer and buy from its rivals. Which impact is this?
options: Loss of customers due to public image
Financial loss due to legal action
D1.3.3.why: A public breach damages trust and reputation, so customers leave.

D2.1.1.q: Everyone in a company can open the payroll spreadsheet, but only HR should be able to edit it. What should be set on the file?
D2.1.1.why: File permissions control who can read, write, run or delete a file.

D2.1.1.q: A teacher can open the shared mark sheet but gets 'access denied' when trying to save changes. What is controlling this?
D2.1.1.why: File permissions decide who can read, write or run each file; this teacher has read but not write.

D2.1.1.q: Which file permission lets a user run a program but not change it?
D2.1.1.why: Execute lets a user run a program; write would let them change it.

D2.1.2.q: Staff should see only their own department's systems, while IT admins can manage everything. Which protection is this?
D2.1.2.why: Access levels give each user only the privileges their role needs.

D2.1.2.q: A new receptionist gets a standard account that can use the booking system but can't install software or change settings. Which protection is this?
D2.1.2.why: Access levels give each role only the systems and privileges its job needs.

D2.1.2.q: Why should IT staff use a standard account for everyday work and an admin account only when needed?
options: If the everyday account is hacked, the attacker gets less access
Standard accounts make the nightly backups run faster
Admin accounts are not allowed to open any email
Using two accounts removes the need for passwords
D2.1.2.why: Least privilege limits the damage if an account is compromised.

D2.1.3.q: A school copies its data every night to a separate location so it can restore files after a disaster. Which protection is this?
D2.1.3.why: Backups are copies kept elsewhere that can be restored after data loss.

D2.1.3.q: A river floods a company's ground-floor server room, destroying all its on-site storage. What should the company have had to survive this?
D2.1.3.why: Natural disasters destroy hardware on site, so only a copy kept somewhere else lets you recover.

D2.1.3.q: A company has backed up every night for a year, but nobody has ever tried restoring from a backup. What is the risk?
options: The backups may be corrupt or incomplete when needed
The backups will slow down the antivirus software
All file permissions will be lost from the backups
Staff biometric data will be exposed by the backups
D2.1.3.why: A backup that has never been tested may not restore, so backups should be tested regularly.

D2.1.4.q: An attacker has stolen a member of staff's password but still can't log in because a code is needed from the staff member's phone. What stopped them?
D2.1.4.why: MFA adds a second factor, so a password alone is not enough.

D2.1.4.q: A website asks for a password and then a code from the user's phone. Why is this more secure than a password alone?
options: It needs two different factors, so a stolen password is not enough
The phone codes can be reused on any other website
It means the password itself can be short and simple
It removes the need for the site to use encryption
D2.1.4.why: MFA needs something you know plus something you have, so an attacker needs both.

D2.1.4.q: How does a password manager improve security?
options: Every account gets a different strong password
It removes the need for multi-factor authentication
It stores passwords in plain text for easy access
It makes every password the same and easy to recall
D2.1.4.why: Password managers stop password reuse, so one leaked password only affects one account.

D2.1.5.q: A lab wants entry that can't be passed on like a swipe card or password, so it scans each person's fingerprint. Which protection is this?
D2.1.5.why: Biometrics use unique body features, which can't easily be shared or forgotten.

D2.1.5.q: Which is a DRAWBACK of biometrics compared with passwords?
options: A stolen fingerprint template can't be changed like a password
They are easy to share with colleagues who need access
They are slower to use than typing a long password
They are easy to forget, like a complex password
D2.1.5.why: You can't change your fingerprint, so stolen biometric data can't be reset.

D2.1.5.q: A phone unlocks only when it recognises its owner's face. Which protection is this?
D2.1.5.why: Biometrics identify people by unique body features such as their face.

D2.1.6.q: A company puts its server room behind a locked door with swipe-card entry and CCTV. Which kind of protection is this?
D2.1.6.why: Physical measures stop unauthorised people reaching IT equipment.

D2.1.6.q: A company makes visitors sign in, wear a badge and be escorted, and keeps the server room locked. Which protection is this?
D2.1.6.why: Physical access control stops unauthorised people reaching IT equipment and data.

D2.1.6.q: How does a swipe-card door system help after a theft from the server room?
options: It logs who entered and when, giving a record to investigate
It encrypts the data stored on the server automatically
It scans the server for malware after each entry
It blocks phishing emails sent to server room staff
D2.1.6.why: Swipe cards both restrict entry and record every entry, so there is evidence if something goes wrong.

D2.1.7.q: A customer checks the padlock on a bank's website to be sure it is the genuine bank. What issued by a Certificate Authority proves this?
D2.1.7.why: Digital certificates prove a website is genuine and enable encryption.

D2.1.7.q: A browser warns that a site's digital certificate has expired. What should the user conclude?
options: The site can't be confirmed as genuine, so avoid entering details
The site has definitely been infected by a virus
Their own password has been stolen by the site
The site is now checking them with biometrics
D2.1.7.why: Certificates prove a site is genuine; an expired one means the browser cannot confirm that.

D2.1.7.q: Who issues the digital certificates that browsers trust?
D2.1.7.why: A trusted Certificate Authority checks the owner's identity before issuing a certificate.

D2.2.q: A downloaded file matches a known trojan's signature and is moved somewhere it can't run. Which software did this, and what action did it take?
D2.2.why: Antivirus finds malware using signatures and behaviour checks, then quarantines or removes it.

D2.2.q: Brand-new malware with no known signature is stopped because the antivirus notices it trying to encrypt hundreds of files. Which feature caught it?
D2.2.why: Heuristics look for suspicious behaviour, so new malware can be caught before a signature exists.

D2.3.q: A business wants to block all incoming network traffic on ports it does not use. What should it configure?
D2.3.why: A firewall monitors traffic in and out and blocks it according to rules.

D2.3.q: Which of these would a firewall NOT stop?
options: A member of staff tricked by a phone call into reading out their password
Incoming traffic on a port the business has closed
Connections from a blocked IP address
An app trying to reach a banned website
D2.3.why: A firewall filters network traffic by rules. Social engineering tricks a person and breaks no traffic rule.

D2.4.1.q: A sales rep's laptop is stolen, but the thief cannot read any of the files on the drive because BitLocker is turned on. What protected the data?
D2.4.1.why: Encrypting stored data means a stolen device or drive can't be read.

D2.4.2.q: Messages are intercepted on public Wi-Fi as they travel, but the attacker sees only scrambled data. What protected them?
D2.4.2.why: Encrypting data as it travels means it can't be read if it is intercepted.

D2.4.2.q: A website publishes a key that anyone can use to encrypt messages to it, but only the website's own secret key can decrypt them. Which type of encryption is this?
D2.4.2.why: Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a matching private key to decrypt, so no secret key has to be shared.

D2.4.3.q: An online shop's checkout page must encrypt card details between the browser and server and prove the site is genuine. What should it use?
D2.4.3.why: HTTPS is HTTP secured with TLS: it encrypts the traffic and proves the server is genuine.

D2.4.3.q: A shopper sees a padlock and https:// in the address bar. What does this confirm?
options: The connection is encrypted and the certificate is valid
The shop is honest and will deliver the goods
The site has been scanned and contains no malware
Payments will be refunded if any fraud happens
D2.4.3.why: HTTPS proves the connection is encrypted and the certificate matches the site. It says nothing about whether the business is trustworthy.
